Alright, the user is still seeing a bunch of UI glitches (text jumping, forced‑top layout) and they also claim the “goal” feature is broken – it isn’t being enhanced as expected. From earlier investigation I know that the goal‑refine step uses a sub‑agent model. In the source I saw two places where a model identifier is hard‑coded:

- In src/tui.tsx line 657 the model is set to "groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant".
- In src/core/config.ts the constant SUBAGENT_MODEL is set to "groq/compound-mini".

I also saw that the chat wrapper in src/core/groq.ts has a function chat(messages, opts) that will be called with the model name supplied in the options. The user’s complaint that “goal didn’t enhance” could be because the model identifier being passed to Groq’s API is wrong – perhaps the API expects the bare model name (e.g. llama-3.1-8b-instant) rather than the prefixed groq/ namespace, or vice‑versa. If the wrong identifier is used, the request could silently fail or fall back to a default, causing the goal refinement to never actually run.

I need to verify which identifier works. The safest way is to make a direct HTTP request to Groq’s chat completion endpoint with a minimal payload (just a “hi” prompt, a tiny max_tokens value) and see if I get a valid JSON response. I’ll try both variants:

1. model: "groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant"
2. model: "llama-3.1-8b-instant"

If one of them succeeds, that tells me which string the API expects. If neither works, maybe the API key is missing or malformed.

Before I can curl, I need the API key. Looking at src/core/config.ts I expect a line like export const GROQ_API_KEY = "gsk_…"; or similar. I’ll grep for any occurrence of “MODEL”, “apiKey”, or “API_KEY” in that file to locate the key definition. Then I’ll extract the literal key (the string that starts with gsk_). However, the key might also be supplied via an environment variable GROQ_API_KEY, which would take precedence in a typical setup. So I’ll write a small shell snippet: first grep the config for the key, strip quotes, assign it to a variable KEY; then if $GROQ_API_KEY is set, override KEY with that. That way the curl commands will always have a valid bearer token.

Finally, I’ll issue the two curl calls, each with the appropriate JSON body, and pipe the output through head -c 300 so I don’t flood the terminal with a huge response – just enough to see whether the request succeeded (e.g. a JSON object with a choices array). I’ll separate the two calls with a newline and include an “===” marker between the grep output and the curl tests for readability.

Putting all of that together, the command I need to run is:

```
grep -n "MODEL\|apiKey\|API_KEY" src/core/config.ts | head
echo ===
KEY=$(grep -o '"gsk_[^"]*"' src/core/config.ts | tr -d '"')
[ -n "$GROQ_API_KEY" ] && KEY=$GROQ_API_KEY
curl -s https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":5}' | head -c 300
echo
curl -s https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"llama-3.1-8b-instant","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":5}' | head -c 300
```

This will give me the key location, confirm I have a token, and show me which model string the API accepts. That information is exactly what I need to diagnose the broken goal‑refine behavior.
